title: Luka Doncic Salary: How to Convert Hourly Pay to Annual Salary in Australia
description: Learn how to convert hourly rates to annual salary using the Luka Doncic salary example. Includes tax, Medicare, super, and Fair Work rates for 2026.
salarySummary: For a standard 38-hour week, annual pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top and tax deducted using 2026–27 resident rates.

faqs.q: How do I convert an hourly rate to an annual salary in Australia?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the hours you work per week, then by 52 weeks. For a full-time 38-hour week, the formula is hourly × 38 × 52. For example, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour gives $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,269.44 per year before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage ($26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026) is the legal minimum for award-free employees. Award rates are higher minimums set by the Fair Work Commission for specific industries and occupations, and they also increased by 4.75% from 1 July 2026. Always check the relevant award using Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied and how does it affect annual pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. For example, the National Minimum Wage casual rate is $26.44 × 1.25 = $33.05 per hour. When converting to annual pay, use the casual rate in the formula: $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,336.80 per year. Super is still paid on the casual rate.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Luka Doncic Salary Conversion

When you hear about a figure like the **Luka Doncic salary**, it’s usually an annual amount. But many Australian workers are paid by the hour, and converting between the two is essential for comparing job offers, budgeting, or understanding your own pay. This guide explains how to convert any hourly rate to an annual salary using the standard 38-hour week, and what to consider for tax, super, and casual loading.

### The Basic Formula

The core conversion is simple: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**. For a full-time employee working 38 hours each week, the calculation becomes:

- Annual gross = hourly rate × 38 × 52

For example, if your hourly rate is $40, your annual salary before tax and super is $40 × 38 × 52 = $79,040. This matches the example in the [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool.

### Why 38 Hours?

In Australia, the standard full-time week under most awards and the National Employment Standards is 38 hours. Some roles use 40 hours, but we assume 38 unless stated otherwise. Always check your award or agreement using the [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman.

### The Fortnightly View

Many Australians are paid fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, simply multiply your weekly pay by 2. Using the $40/hour example:

- Weekly: $40 × 38 = $1,520
- Fortnightly: $1,520 × 2 = $3,040

This is useful for budgeting between pay cycles.

## National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is **$26.44 per hour** or **$1,004.90 per week** for a 38-hour week, according to the Fair Work Ombudsman. Award minimum wages increased by 4.75% on the same date. The National Minimum Wage applies to employees not covered by an award or agreement. Most workers are covered by an award, which sets higher minimum rates for their industry or role. Always check the relevant [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page for your classification.

### Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (sick leave, annual leave). The casual rate is calculated as:

- Casual rate = base hourly rate × 1.25

For the National Minimum Wage, the casual rate is $26.44 × 1.25 = **$33.05 per hour**. When converting to annual pay, use the casual rate in the formula. For example, a casual on the minimum wage earns $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,336.80 per year (before tax and super). Our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains this in more detail.

**Important:** Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading into a calculator that adds it again. If you are a casual employee, use your base rate and let the calculator apply the loading.

## Superannuation: Paid on Top

Superannuation (super) is paid by your employer on top of your ordinary earnings. From 1 July 2026, the Super Guarantee rate is **12%** of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of **$270,830** per year. Super is not deducted from your pay; it’s an additional contribution to your super fund.

For the $40/hour example:

- Annual ordinary earnings: $79,040
- Super (12%): $9,484.80
- Total cost to employer: $88,524.80

Super is not included in the annual salary figure you see on a contract. When comparing a salary offer to an hourly rate, remember that the salary usually excludes super, while the hourly rate may or may not include it. Always clarify.

## Tax and Medicare Levy

Your annual gross pay is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: Nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% of excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 + 30% of excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 + 37% of excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,420 + 45% of excess over $190,000

The Medicare levy is generally **2%** of your taxable income. Low-income earners may be eligible for a reduction or exemption. For the 2025–26 year, the single reduction threshold was $24,276; the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this guide, so our calculator uses the 2025–26 figures as a conservative estimate.

Using the $79,040 annual gross example:

- Tax: ($79,040 – $45,000) × 0.30 + $4,020 = $34,040 × 0.30 + $4,020 = $10,212 + $4,020 = $14,232
- Medicare levy (2%): $79,040 × 0.02 = $1,580.80
- Total deductions: $15,812.80
- Net annual pay: $79,040 – $15,812.80 = $63,227.20

This is your take-home pay before any other deductions like HELP loans or salary packaging. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator for a more detailed estimate.

## Putting It All Together: The Luka Doncic Salary Example

Let’s apply this to a hypothetical scenario. If Luka Doncic were paid an hourly rate in Australia (unlikely, but instructive), say **$100 per hour** on a 38-hour week:

- Annual gross: $100 × 38 × 52 = $197,600
- Fortnightly gross: ($100 × 38) × 2 = $7,600
- Super (12%): $23,712 (but capped at $270,830 contribution base – well within limit)
- Tax (2026–27): $31,020 + 37% of ($197,600 – $135,000) = $31,020 + $23,162 = $54,182
- Medicare levy (2%): $3,952
- Net annual pay: $197,600 – $54,182 – $3,952 = $139,466

This shows how a high hourly rate translates to a substantial annual salary, but also significant tax obligations. The **Luka Doncic salary** example helps illustrate the conversion process for any rate.

## Important Disclaimer

Annual pay calculated here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For personalised advice, consult a registered tax agent or the Australian Taxation Office. Use our [reference tables](/data) for more detailed rate information.
